summary:
Gravity Gap is a web dashboard that turns NASA's microgravity combustion data into fire-safety answers for the places crews will live next: the Moon and Mars. Every fire test in NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics archive was run either in orbit or on Earth, leaving lunar and Martian gravity, and the 8.2 psia, 34% oxygen air planned for exploration habitats, almost untested.

Gravity Gap summarizes, ranks and interprets 1,710 real PSI combustion tests. A physics engine and statistical models predict how fires behave in any habitat, each with an uncertainty band that widens across the gravity gap. Where the evidence runs out, it refuses to guess and shows "no evidence" instead. It produces a printable fire-safety briefing per habitat, tests its own accuracy against hidden experiments, and ranks the experiments NASA should run next. An AI assistant explains results, but every number it uses must trace back to a NASA test.

This matters because fire is one of the deadliest hazards in space, and lunar habitats are being designed now.
details:
What it does

Gravity Gap predicts how a fire would behave inside a Moon or Mars habitat, using NASA’s real fire experiments. It also shows how sure it is, and refuses to guess when the evidence runs out.

Every fire test in NASA’s Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) archive was run at one of two gravities: in orbit (about 0 g) or on Earth (1 g). The Moon (1.62 m/s²) and Mars (3.71 m/s²) sit in the gap between them, and NASA’s planned exploration habitat air (8.2 psia, 34% oxygen) has barely been tested. Crews will live in exactly that gap, so Gravity Gap is built to answer the question: what does the evidence say about fire there, and where does it say nothing?

How it works

  1. Pick a habitat: the ISS, a lunar base, a lunar rover, a Mars base, Earth, or your own gravity, cabin pressure, oxygen level and ventilation speed.
  2. Flame physics: the engine works out how strongly the flame’s own buoyancy competes with the cabin fan, and classifies the flame as forced-flow, mixed or buoyant. At a lunar base it is mixed, the hardest case to predict.
  3. Statistical models fitted to 1,710 cleaned NASA PSI combustion tests (FLEX droplet flames, ACME burner flames, SAFFIRE large-scale fires and others) give estimates for five fire behaviours. Each estimate has a 90% uncertainty band, and a Monte Carlo analysis over the physics assumptions widens that band to account for the gravity difference.
  4. An honesty gate measures how far the habitat’s air is from the nearest air NASA actually tested. If it is too far, the app shows “no evidence” and names the nearest test instead of printing a number. At the lunar base it gives a droplet flame a 20% chance of going out on its own (90% band 1.2% to 68%), but refuses three of its five metrics. For example, the nearest test for extinction diameter is at distance 2.14, past the 2.0 limit.
  5. The tool checks itself. A hold-out “honesty test” hides tested atmospheres, refits the models and checks whether the bands still caught the real results. The results are published as they came out, misses included. A hindcast of NASA’s SAFFIRE experiments is also included.

Main features

  • Bounds: estimates with their bands, and a breakdown of what makes each band wide.
  • Compare: two habitats side by side.
  • Air map: which oxygen and pressure combinations NASA’s evidence covers, with NASA crew health limits drawn from NASA-STD-3001.
  • Briefing: a one-page, printable fire-safety briefing per habitat.
  • Trust: the honesty test.
  • Planner: a ranked list of the tests NASA should run next to close the gap.
  • Replay: real spacecraft fire incidents (Apollo 1, Mir 1997, the Artemis II smoke alarm) loaded as habitats.
  • Put it out and Detection: what NASA’s data says about suppressing fires by dilution, and about smoke particle sizes.
  • Ask: an AI assistant that may only use numbers from the engine and must cite the NASA test or result behind each claim. An automatic validator rejects any number or citation it can’t trace.

Benefits and intended impact

  • Habitat and fire-safety engineers get one honest view of what is known, what is estimated and what is unknown about fire at partial gravity, before the habitats are built.
  • Instead of hiding uncertainty, Gravity Gap turns it into a research plan. Its top-ranked test targets exactly the lunar base air where the evidence runs out.
  • Our goal is to help NASA and its partners prioritize the next partial-gravity combustion experiments, and to make NASA’s open fire data usable by people who aren’t combustion specialists.
  • It is decision support for research planning, not a safety certification, and it says so on every page.

How it is creative

  • Most tools give an answer. Gravity Gap is designed to refuse one, visibly, when the data doesn’t support it. That refusal is its central feature.
  • It pre-registers its own predictions in a hash-verified, append-only ledger, so they can be checked when future lunar experiments fly.
  • It tests itself in public.
  • The website tells the story visually. A real Apollo 11 Earthrise photo is used as a layered parallax scene. A to-scale gravity axis shows the Moon and Mars landing in the empty span between NASA’s tests, and a “No evidence” stamp lands where the data stops.

Factors we considered

  • Scientific honesty: every number traces to a NASA test or an engine output. Uncertainty is shown, never hidden.
  • Physics: buoyancy, ventilation, gravity, pressure and oxygen, including the higher-oxygen air planned for exploration habitats.
  • Data quality: NASA’s spreadsheets were cleaned, with every fix recorded. Values like “LOW O2” or “#DIV/0!” were flagged and excluded rather than guessed.
  • Safety wording: CO₂ and helium suppression results carry safety notes, so nothing reads as an operating procedure.
  • Accessibility: automated WCAG accessibility checks pass on every page in both light and dark themes.
  • Reliability: the site works without a backend by serving the saved engine outputs.

Tools, languages and software

  • Python: physics engine, Monte Carlo, statistical models, data cleaning, a FastAPI backend and pytest tests.
  • TypeScript: Next.js 15 and React with Tailwind CSS, hand-built SVG charts, and Vitest and Playwright tests (including automated accessibility checks).
  • Infrastructure: GitHub Actions continuous integration and Docker, deployed on Vercel.
  • Demo video: Remotion.
  • Data: NASA PSI combustion data (CC0) via the PSI API, NASA-STD-3001 Vol. 2 crew health limits, NASA technical reports, and public-domain NASA photos (credited, with no NASA logos).
  • No special hardware.
  • AI assistance: we used Anthropic’s Claude (via Claude Code) to help write the code, tests and documentation. The fire-safety numbers themselves come from the physics engine and statistical models fitted to NASA data, not from a language model. The app’s optional AI assistant only restates validated engine outputs.
